verified.notes: Checked 16 Nov 2026 (checker agent on Fable; 60 blocks, prompts, options and 18 map elements; Livy lat3, lat2 at 10.19.22, Roberts, Ovid, Pliny, Smith and Pleiades opened). All nine Latin quotations, every figure and every Livy locator matched. Fixed 3 errors and 18 lesser points with the checker's wording, without a second pass: Smith's entry is no. 10 (the '11' was a Perseus file id); Camerinum removed from the map (no passage in Livy 10.16–31 names it); the caption no longer says Umbria's lettering stands on its Pleiades point; the unlocated-towns box moved off the sea; 'all year', 'again' and 'by different ways' cut where the Latin lacks them. The elogium of Appius Claudius could not be opened in any edition and is not quoted. Researcher's draft notes (2026-11-16). Livy cited by the Conway–Walters (OCT) section numbers in Perseus lat3; Weissenborn–Müller (lat2) compared at 10.19.22 only. Roberts 1912 (Perseus eng3) numbers several sections differently in 10.16–10.21 (his 10.16.2 runs into OCT 10.16.3; his 10.18.2 = OCT 10.18.1 end and 10.18.2; his 10.18.1–2: OCT 10.18.1 ends inside his 10.18.2; his 10.18.6 runs on through OCT 10.18.7 as far as 'fungentes', his 10.18.7 is the rest; his 10.19.14–15 = OCT 10.19.14; his 10.19.21 begins at OCT 10.19.20 'ibi interventu Gelli'; his 10.19.22 begins at OCT 10.19.21 'per vallum'; his 10.19.16–17 = OCT 10.19.16–17 shifted by a clause; his 10.20.8–9 = OCT 10.20.8). Roberts is quoted once, at 10.20.8 (first sentence), where he is accurate; elsewhere the English is ours because he is loose: 'some annalists' for 'in trinis annalibus' (10.18.7), 'a peace which reduced them to slavery … a war in which they could fight as free men' (10.16.5), 'a war chest' for 'stipendio' (10.16.8), 'the country round Capua' for 'in Campaniam' and 'feudatories of Rome' for 'imperii Romani fines' (10.20.1), 'Menturna' (10.21.8), 'Statius Minacius' (10.20.13), and 6,900 dead at 10.19.22 where the Oxford text prints 'septem milia octingenti'. Perseus lat3 layout and OCR fixes in passages quoted: the OCT margin 'A.U.C. 458' interleaved in 10.16.3 and 10.19.17 removed; 'Bellona , si' closed up (10.19.17); the apparatus notes at 10.18.7 removed from the quotation and reported in card-letter. Not quoted but seen: 'donec done' (10.16.2), 'haud baud' (10.16.5, 10.17.6), 'opulentissimam oppulentissimam' (10.16.6), 'Samnitibus Sannitibus' and 'tusci' (10.18.1–2), 'huc hue' (10.18.13), 'tumultu tunultu' (10.20.11). Ovid, Fasti, from Perseus lat2 (ed. J. G. Frazer); lines 6.199–208 read; we did not work out the calendar day from the preceding lines, so the card says only 'on this day' and that the passage stands in the book for June. Pliny, Natural History 35.12, from Perseus lat2 (ed. K. Mayhoff): the square brackets round 'qui consul … CCLVIIII' are in the file, with an apparatus note 'uncos posuit U cum Gesnero' and a marginal 'cfr. Liv. X 19, 17'; we did not open Mayhoff's list of sigla, so 'U' is not expanded. The elogium of Appius Claudius Caecus (the Arretium copy) could not be opened in any edition or database, so neither its text nor a corpus number is given; the only trace used is Smith's reference 'Orelli, Inscr. No. 539', cited as Smith's. Each decision has one historical option and two counterfactuals (no alternative advice is recorded for either). Years BC are the conventional ones; 'last year' rests on Livy's sequence of consular years (297 Fabius–Decius, 296 Volumnius–Claudius). The story stops at Volumnius' recall for the elections (10.21.13); the consuls of 295 are left to scene 7.

Ovid.label: Ovid, Fasti (Latin, ed. J. G. Frazer; Perseus Digital Library)

Pliny.label: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis historia (Latin, ed. K. Mayhoff, Teubner; Perseus Digital Library)

Smith.label: W. Smith (ed.), A Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology, s.v. Claudius no. 10, App. Claudius Caecus (Perseus text of the 1873 printing)

Pleiades.label: Pleiades gazetteer of ancient places (place records, via isawnyu/pleiades.datasets)

blocks.text: Samnium, 296 BC. Last year two consular armies ranged over different parts of Samnium for five months and laid everything waste. Forty-five places are counted where Decius pitched camp, eighty-six for Fabius.

This year the new consuls at Rome are L. Volumnius and Ap. Claudius. The old ones have been kept in command for six months to carry on the war in Samnium. P. Decius, now proconsul, has not stopped wasting your fields. Your army has nowhere trusted itself to a battle.

Your envoys have often tried the Etruscans, and always in vain. Last year envoys from Sutrium, Nepete and Falerii reported at Rome that the peoples of Etruria were holding councils about asking for peace.
The game seats you among the elders of the touto, whose counsel the commanders ask.

steps.prompt: Decius is driving the army out of Samnium. It has nowhere risked a battle. Where should it go?

options.label: To Etruria, the whole army. Ask in arms for what our envoys asked in vain.

consequence.text: Driven from its own land, the army makes for Etruria and demands a council of the Etruscan leaders. A column of armed men this size, it reckons, will do more than embassies did, with menace mixed into the asking.

quote.la: Etruriam pulsi petierunt, et quod legationibus nequiquam saepe temptaverant, id se tanto agmine armatorum mixtis terrore precibus acturos efficacius rati, postulaverunt principum Etruriae concilium.
quote.en: Driven out, they made for Etruria; and reckoning that what they had often tried in vain by embassies they would bring about more effectively with so great a column of armed men, mixing menace with entreaty, they demanded a council of the leading men of Etruria.
quote.it: Scacciati, si diressero in Etruria; e ritenendo che ciò che avevano spesso tentato invano con le ambascerie l'avrebbero ottenuto più efficacemente con una così grande colonna di armati, mescolando il terrore alle preghiere, chiesero un'assemblea dei capi dell'Etruria.

consequence.note: The Perseus text interleaves the OCT margin 'A.U.C. 458' in this sentence; removed. Roberts divides the sentence between his 10.16.2 and 10.16.3; the English is ours.

consequence.text: Behind you, Decius learns from his scouts that the army has gone. He stops raiding farms and turns on the towns.

options.label: Nowhere. Stay in Samnium and keep refusing battle.
options.kind_note: No Samnite is recorded proposing this

consequence.text: Refusing battle is what the army has been doing, and it has ended with the army pushed over its own border.
Once the army is gone, the Roman commander draws his conclusion.

quote.la: quid per agros inquit vagamur vicatim circumferentes bellum? quin urbes et moenia adgredimur? nullus iam exercitus Samnio praesidet
quote.en: 'Why', he said, 'do we wander through the fields, carrying the war round village by village? Why do we not attack cities and walls? No army now guards Samnium.'
quote.it: «Perché», disse, «vaghiamo per i campi portando la guerra di villaggio in villaggio? Perché non assaliamo città e mura? Nessun esercito ormai presidia il Sannio.»

consequence.note: A speech composed for Decius. Roberts has 'making war only upon the villages' and 'the walled cities'; the English is ours.

consequence.text: Whether an army that would not fight could have stayed in Samnium, or kept the towns by staying, no source can tell us.

options.label: Down into Campania, through the land of the Vescini, for plunder.
options.kind_note: What new Samnite armies did later this year; not proposed for this army

consequence.text: Later this year new armies raised in Samnium do exactly this, while both consuls are in Etruria. They take great plunder, and are caught with it on the Volturnus.
Whether the main army would have fared better there, with Decius behind it, no source can tell us.

outcome.text: The Samnite army, driven out of Samnium by the proconsul Decius, went to Etruria and demanded a council of the Etruscan leaders.

blocks.text: Livy names no route and no meeting place. Before the Etruscan council the Samnites set out how many years they had fought Rome for their freedom. The argument Livy gives them: they had tried everything to carry the war on their own strength; the help of neighbouring peoples had counted for little; their one hope left was the Etruscans, the richest people of Italy in arms, men and money, with the Gauls for neighbours.

quote.la: petisse pacem a populo Romano, cum bellum tolerare non possent; rebellasse, quod pax servientibus gravior quam liberis bellum esset.
quote.en: They had sought peace from the Roman people when they could not bear the war; they had gone to war again because peace was heavier for men in servitude than war for free men.
quote.it: Avevano chiesto la pace al popolo romano, non potendo sostenere la guerra; avevano ripreso le armi perché la pace era più gravosa per chi serve che la guerra per chi è libero.

blocks.note: Reported speech, composed by Livy. Roberts expands: 'a peace which reduced them to slavery … a war in which they could fight as free men'; the English is ours.

blocks.text: They offered an army ready, armed and bringing its own pay, which would follow the Etruscans at once, even to an attack on Rome itself. Livy does not report the council's answer. Later he says that a huge war was being raised against Rome in Etruria from many peoples, and names its author: Gellius Egnatius, of the Samnites. Nearly all the Etruscans had resolved on war, the nearest peoples of Umbria were drawn in, Gallic auxiliaries were being sought for hire, and the whole multitude gathered at the Samnite camp.

quote.la: Samnitem illis exercitum paratum, instructum armis, stipendio venisse, et confestim secuturos, vel si ad ipsam Romanam urbem oppugnandam ducant.
quote.en: A Samnite army had come to them ready, furnished with arms and with pay, and they would follow at once, even if the Etruscans led them to attack the city of Rome itself.
quote.it: Un esercito sannita era venuto da loro pronto, provvisto di armi e di paga, e li avrebbero seguiti subito, anche se li avessero condotti ad assalire la stessa città di Roma.

blocks.note: Roberts has 'a war chest' for stipendio; the English is ours.

blocks.text: Central Italy in 296 BC, from Samnium to Etruria and Umbria. A map of what Livy names for this year, not of a march: he gives no route to Etruria, so none is drawn, and no place for the Etruscan council or the Samnite camp, so they are a box, not a point. Murgantia, Romulea and Ferentinum, the towns stormed in Samnium, have no site in Pleiades and share a second box. Rome, Cales, Minturnae and the ager Falernus are placed from Pleiades; the Volturnus is a name only, set on Pleiades' point for the river, and its course is not drawn. The region names stand on its points for Etruria and Samnium; Umbria's is moved south of its point to clear the town names. In grey, for the year that follows: Clusium, Perusia and the land of Sentinum, which Livy names in the next campaign. Ours: the positions of the two boxes, the place of the Umbria lettering, the choice to show next year's places in grey, the sea names and the scale bar.

figure.alt: Map of central Italy. Samnium is lettered in the south-east, with Cales, the ager Falernus, the name of the river Volturnus and Minturnae near the west coast below it. Rome stands in the middle of the west coast. Etruria and Umbria are lettered to the north, with Clusium, Perusia and Sentinum in grey. A dashed box in Etruria reads: Etruscan council and Samnite camp, 296, place not given. A second dashed box north of the Samnium lettering reads: Murgantia, Romulea, Ferentinum, sites unknown. No route is drawn.
figure.credit: Sites from the Pleiades gazetteer (CC BY); coastline Natural Earth (public domain).

blocks.note: Drawn by tools/maps/coalition_map.py. Pleiades has no position for Murgantia (438790) or for its unlocated Ferentinum (438734), and calls Romulea unlocated (438820, 446286). The Pleiades record for Sinuessa was not found, so the second colony is not drawn.

blocks.text: In Samnium Decius stormed Murgantia in a single day, then Romulea by escalade, then Ferentinum, which cost more. Livy's figures: 2,100 taken at Murgantia; some 2,300 killed and 6,000 taken at Romulea; some 3,000 killed round the walls of Ferentinum. He adds that some annals give most of this to Fabius, and others to the new consuls, or to Volumnius alone.

When the news from Etruria reached Rome, Volumnius had already left for Samnium with the second and third legions and fifteen thousand allies. Ap. Claudius was sent to Etruria at once, with the first and fourth legions and twelve thousand allies, and camped not far from the enemy. In Livy's judgement his early arrival checked some Etruscan peoples already looking to arms; his generalship did little. He fought many actions at the wrong place and time, and the enemy grew more formidable by the day.
Later in 296. Volumnius has left Samnium, where he had taken three strongholds, and marched to join his colleague in Etruria. Decius is left to waste your fields.

In Etruria the two consuls have fought together. Gellius Egnatius was away foraging with a few cohorts when the battle began, and the men went into it on their own impulse, with no one in command. The Etruscans met Volumnius; the Samnites, after hesitating because their leader was absent, met Appius. Gellius came up with his Sabellian cohorts when the line had been driven back to the camp, and the fight flared again briefly. The camp was stormed and plundered.
Now both consuls and the whole strength of Rome lean toward the Etruscan war. In Samnium new armies have been raised.

steps.prompt: Both consuls are in Etruria. New armies have been raised at home. What should they do?

options.label: Cross through the Vescini into Campania and the Falernian land, and plunder Rome's territory.

consequence.text: The armies cross through the Vescini into Campania and the Falernian land and take huge plunder.

Volumnius is already marching back to Samnium by forced marches, since the extended commands of Fabius and Decius are running out. Word of the raid turns him aside to protect the allies. In the land of Cales he sees the fresh damage himself, and the people of Cales tell him that the raiders are dragging so much plunder they can hardly form their column.
The Roman theatre at Cales, photographed in 2012. Rome had taken Cales in 335 BC and planted a colony there. The theatre belongs to the first century BC, two centuries and more after the raid.
consequence.note: Commons files the photograph under 'Teatro Romano di Cales'; its description reads 'Incontri al Teatro -Cales 2012-'. Pleiades 432739 gives the capture as 335 BC and the colony; Pleiades 926867727 dates the theatre to the first century BC. Livy's own account of the capture and colony (book 8) was not opened for this caption. Pleiades read in isawnyu/pleiades.datasets places.csv; pleiades.stoa.org not opened.

figure.alt: A field of cut yellow grass in front of the curved, ruined seating of a theatre in rough stone and brick, with a few arched openings, under a cloudy sky.
figure.credit: Photo: PietroCifone, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized.

consequence.text: Your leaders, they say, now talk openly: go back to Samnium at once, leave the plunder there, come back for another raid, and do not risk so loaded a column in a fight.

options.label: Send them north to Gellius Egnatius. The war will be decided in Etruria.
options.kind_note: No Samnite is recorded proposing this

consequence.text: After Volumnius takes his army out of Etruria, the report at Rome is that Etruria is roused to arms, that Gellius Egnatius and the Umbrians are being called to revolt, and that the Gauls are being sought at a huge price.
consequence.note: The Latin sets 'Gellium Egnatium, Samnitium ducem, et Umbros' together as objects of 'ad defectionem vocari'; Roberts has the country rising 'in concert with' him.

consequence.text: Later Appius writes that four peoples are joining arms, Etruscans, Samnites, Umbrians and Gauls, and that they have already made two camps, since one place cannot hold such a multitude.
Whether more Samnites in those camps would have changed anything, no source can tell us.

options.label: Keep them in Samnium and turn them on Decius, who has been left there.
options.kind_note: No Samnite is recorded proposing this

consequence.text: Decius has been left in Samnium to waste the fields. The extended commands of Fabius and Decius are close to their end.
Whether new levies could have beaten the army that had driven the old one out of Samnium, no source can tell us.

outcome.text: New Samnite armies crossed through the Vescini into Campania and the Falernian land and took great plunder. Volumnius, on his way back from Etruria, caught them leaving their camp on the Volturnus.

blocks.text: From stragglers picked up by his cavalry Volumnius learned that the raiders sat on the Volturnus and would move at the third watch, for Samnium. He camped far enough off not to be noticed and came up to their camp before dawn.

quote.la: aliquanto ante lucem ad castra accessit gnarosque Oscae linguae exploratum quid agatur mittit.
quote.en: Some time before daylight he approached their camp and sent some men familiar with the Oscan language to find out what was going on.
quote.it: Alquanto prima dell'alba si avvicinò al campo e mandò uomini che conoscevano la lingua osca a esplorare che cosa si facesse.

blocks.text: Mixed in with the enemy in the confusion of the night, they found the standards gone out with few armed men about them, the plunder and its guards on the way out, the column stuck, each man busy with his own, and no firm command. Volumnius attacked at first light. The prisoners in the column broke loose, armed themselves from the baggage, seized the Samnite commander Staius Minatius on his horse and carried him to the consul.

Livy's figures: about 6,000 killed and 2,500 captured, four military tribunes among them; thirty standards; 7,400 captives recovered, with a great mass of the allies' property, which the owners were summoned by edict to identify.

The raid had caused great alarm at Rome, and in the same days came the report from Etruria that the country was up in arms once Volumnius' army had gone. The Senate ordered a iustitium and a levy of every kind of man: cohorts of older men were formed and freedmen enrolled in centuries, and the praetor P. Sempronius had charge of the city. Volumnius' letter lifted part of the fear; the iustitium had lasted eighteen days. The Senate then resolved on two colonies for the wasted district, Minturnae and Sinuessa.

Minturnae, the colony voted that year for the mouth of the Liris, the modern Garigliano, photographed in 2014: the forum, with the theatre behind it. The theatre was built under Augustus or Tiberius, nearly three centuries later; the photograph's record calls the forum in front of it Republican, without a closer date.
blocks.note: The Commons title says the theatre was 'built in the late Republican ear [sic] or at the beginning of the Empire'; Pleiades 658246004 says it was built under Augustus or Tiberius and embellished under Hadrian. The caption follows Pleiades. 'ad ostium Liris fluvii' is Livy 10.21.8. Pleiades 432940: Minturnae 'became a colony in 296 B.C.' and is located on the Garigliano (ancient Liris). The paved street in the photograph is not identified in its record. Pleiades read in isawnyu/pleiades.datasets places.csv; pleiades.stoa.org not opened.

figure.alt: Toppled column drums and squared stone blocks lie beside a paved street. Behind them rise the curved stone seats of a theatre, with brick arches at one end, under a blue sky with clouds.
figure.credit: Photo: Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized.

blocks.text: Appius kept writing from Etruria: four peoples were joining arms, Etruscans, Samnites, Umbrians and Gauls, and they had already made two camps. Volumnius was called back to Rome for the elections. The scene stops there.
At the crisis of the battle in Etruria Appius is said to have raised his hands to the sky among the front standards, where he could be seen, and prayed.

quote.la: Bellona, si hodie nobis victoriam duis, ast ego tibi templum voveo.
quote.en: Bellona, if today you give us victory, then I vow you a temple.
quote.it: Bellona, se oggi ci dai la vittoria, io ti voto un tempio.

blocks.note: Livy reports the prayer with 'dicitur'. The Perseus text interleaves the OCT margin 'A.U.C. 458' and prints 'Bellona , si'; tidied. Roberts adds 'in return'; the English is ours.

blocks.text: Ovid, in the book of his Fasti for June, has the same founder and the same war.

quote.la: hac sacrata die Tusco Bellona duello / dicitur et Latio prospera semper adest. / Appius est auctor, Pyrrho qui pace negata / multum animo vidit, lumine captus erat.
quote.en: On this day, it is said, Bellona was consecrated in the Etruscan war, and she is always favourable to Latium. Her founder is Appius, who, when peace was refused to Pyrrhus, saw much with his mind, though he had lost his sight.
quote.it: In questo giorno, si dice, fu consacrata Bellona nella guerra etrusca, ed è sempre propizia al Lazio. Ne è autore Appio, che, negata la pace a Pirro, molto vide con l'animo, privo com'era della vista.

blocks.note: Ovid too writes 'dicitur'. He calls the war Etruscan and does not name the Samnites.

blocks.text: Ovid adds that a small open space before the temple looks toward the top of the Circus, and that a small column stands there, from which the spear that announces war is thrown when arms are to be taken up against a king and peoples.

Pliny found a record that an Appius Claudius was the first to dedicate shields privately in a sacred or public place: he set up his ancestors in the temple of Bellona, to be seen on high and the inscriptions of their offices read.

quote.la: Verum clupeos in sacro vel publico dicare privatim primus instituit, ut reperio, Appius Claudius [qui consul cum P. Servilio fuit anno urbis CCLVIIII]. posuit enim in Bellonae aede maiores suos
quote.en: But the first to begin dedicating shields in a sacred or public place on his own account was, as I find, Appius Claudius [who was consul with P. Servilius in the 259th year of the city]. For he set up his ancestors in the temple of Bellona
quote.it: Ma il primo a dedicare scudi a titolo privato in luogo sacro o pubblico fu, a quanto trovo, Appio Claudio [che fu console con P. Servilio nell'anno 259 della città]. Pose infatti i suoi antenati nel tempio di Bellona

blocks.text: The words in brackets make this Appius a consul of the city's 259th year, about two centuries before the year the Oxford margin gives for the vow, A.U.C. 458. Mayhoff's text prints them in square brackets, and a note of his refers to Livy 10.19.17. Which Appius Claudius hung the shields is not settled by anything we have opened.
cites: Pliny, Natural History 35.12 (Mayhoff, text and apparatus)
blocks.note: Mayhoff's note on the brackets reads 'uncos posuit U cum Gesnero'; we have not opened his list of sigla.

blocks.text: Did Appius write to call Volumnius out of Samnium? Livy found the letter in three annals and still would not vouch for it.

quote.la: litteras ad collegam accersendum ex Samnio missas in trinis annalibus invenio; piget tamen in certo ponere, cum ea ipsa inter consules populi Romani, iam iterum eodem honore fungentes, disceptatio fuerit, Appio abnuente missas, Volumnio adfirmante Appi se litteris accitum.
quote.en: I find in three annals that a letter was sent to summon his colleague from Samnium; yet I am loath to set it down as certain, since this very point was in dispute between consuls of the Roman people, now holding the same office for the second time, Appius denying that it was sent, Volumnius affirming that he had been summoned by Appius' letter.
quote.it: Trovo in tre annali che fu mandata una lettera per chiamare il collega dal Sannio; mi rincresce tuttavia darlo per certo, poiché proprio questo fu oggetto di disputa tra i consoli del popolo romano, che ricoprivano ormai per la seconda volta la stessa carica: Appio negava che fosse stata mandata, Volumnio affermava di essere stato chiamato da una lettera di Appio.

blocks.note: Roberts has 'some annalists' for 'in trinis annalibus'; the English is ours.

blocks.text: 'In certo' is Walters' reading. The Oxford apparatus gives the manuscripts' reading as 'incertum' and records another conjecture, 'id certum'. For 'disceptatio' it reports that most manuscripts have 'discrepatio'.

Livy then gives his own guess, marked as one: Appius' temper came from his conscience. He was justly angry if he had written nothing; if he had needed the help, he was hiding it in a mean and ungrateful spirit.

As Livy tells the meeting, Appius asked what had brought Volumnius out of his province. Volumnius answered that things in Samnium went well and that he had come at Appius' letter; if it was false he would turn his standards about at once. The legates and tribunes of Appius' army stopped him, and the soldiers shouted for both consuls to fight the Etruscan war together.

Pleiades gives none of the three a site. It calls Murgantia strongly fortified, taken by Decius, and now unlocated; it calls Romulea now unlocated, though it carries a rough point for it; and it has an unlocated Ferentinum from sheet 44 of the Barrington Atlas, separate from the Hernican Ferentinum on the Via Latina.

Livy makes the plunder the method. After Murgantia Decius has the booty sold, so that the column is not loaded with baggage, and tells the men to draw the trader after the army with the profit: he will keep them supplied with things to sell. The same is done after Romulea.

Livy did not know who commanded. In some annals most of the credit goes to Fabius: Murgantia to Decius, Ferentinum and Romulea to Fabius. Others give it to the new consuls, and some to one of them only, L. Volumnius, to whom they say Samnium had fallen as his province. Livy moves on with the words 'under whoever's command and auspices'.
The praenomen L. is Sigonius' correction; the Oxford apparatus gives the manuscripts' reading as p. and refers to CIL I² p. 132.

Smith's Dictionary has Appius himself command 'at first in Samnium with some success' in this consulship, citing Livy 10.17 and an inscription, Orelli no. 539. We could not open that inscription in any edition, so its words are not given here.
cites: Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1873 printing), s.v. Claudius no. 10

blocks.text: Livy numbers the legions of the year: the second and third with Volumnius, with fifteen thousand allies; the first and fourth with Appius, with twelve thousand.

For the battle in Etruria the Oxford text prints 7,800 enemy dead and 2,120 prisoners. Its apparatus marks 'octingenti' as the editors' reading; the Perseus transcription gives the manuscripts as 'accc' or 'acccc', which we have not checked against the printed page. Weissenborn–Müller prints the same 7,800. Roberts' translation has 6,900 killed.
In Samnium before he left, Volumnius took three strongholds, with about 3,000 killed and about half as many captured, on Livy's figures.

On the Volturnus: about 6,000 killed, 2,500 captured, thirty standards, 7,400 captives recovered. Whatever found no owner by the day set was given to the soldiers, who were made to sell it, so that their minds should be on nothing but their arms.
Livy first names him as the author of the war in Etruria, 'ex Samnitibus'. He does not say that Egnatius led the march from Samnium, or that he spoke before the Etruscan council.

In the battle against the two consuls he is 'Samnitium dux', away foraging with a few cohorts when it began; he came up with 'Sabellian cohorts' when the line had been driven to the camp. In the report that reached Rome later in the year he is again 'Samnitium dux'.

Money runs through Livy's account of the coalition. The Samnite army came with its pay; the Gallic auxiliaries were sought 'mercede', for hire, and later 'pretio ingenti', at a huge price. He names no sums.
The commander taken on the Volturnus is printed Staius Minatius in the Oxford text. Roberts' translation has Statius Minacius.

After the raid the Senate resolved on two colonies about the Vescine and Falernian land: one at the mouth of the Liris, called Minturnae; the other in the saltus Vescinus where it touches the Falernian land, where a Greek city Sinope is said to have stood, named Sinuessa by the Roman colonists.
blocks.note: The Oxford text prints Sigonius' 'Vescinos' at 10.20.1 for the manuscripts' 'uestinos', and 'Vescinum' and 'Vescino' here on the same ground.

blocks.text: The tribunes of the plebs were charged with a plebiscite ordering the praetor P. Sempronius to appoint three commissioners to lead the colonists out. Volunteers were hard to find.

quote.la: nec qui nomina darent facile inveniebantur, quia in stationem se prope perpetuam infestae regionis, non in agros mitti rebantur.
quote.en: Nor were men easily found to give in their names, because they reckoned they were being sent to an all but permanent outpost in a hostile region, not onto land.
quote.it: Né si trovava facilmente chi desse il proprio nome, perché ritenevano di essere mandati a un presidio quasi perpetuo in una regione infestata dai nemici, non nei campi.

blocks.text: Pleiades places Minturnae on the Garigliano, the ancient Liris, and dates the colony to 296 BC.
The district stays a target. In the next year, on Livy's account, Samnites again came down to plunder the Vescine and Formian land, and elsewhere the land of Aesernia and along the Volturnus.
